question: What does Madhyamaka reasoning negate: inherent existence only, or all four extremes including existence itself?

sides.position: The object of negation is inherent existence (existence from the object's own side, not posited by conceptual designation). Things are not negated conventionally; emptiness is a non-affirming negation of inherent existence, and conventional existence, cause and effect and valid cognition remain. To negate existence as such is to negate too much and fall into nihilism.
arguments: If the negandum is not identified one cannot ascertain its absence (the thief and the house).
Not being found by ultimate analysis is not the same as being refuted by it.
Nāgārjuna's and Candrakīrti's negations of arising etc. carry an implicit qualifier 'ultimately / inherently' made explicit by the Prāsaṅgika commentators.

sides.position: The final view is freedom from elaborations: at the level of ultimate analysis all four extremes — existence, non-existence, both, neither — are negated without qualification, and clinging to emptiness as a mere negation is itself an extreme; Tsongkhapa's system, by adding the qualifier and holding the ultimate to be a non-affirming negation, is 'Madhyamaka of the nihilist extreme' and also leaves a subtle grasping.
arguments: Nāgārjuna and Candrakīrti negate arising without qualification.
Emptiness as an object of a conceptual negation is still an elaboration.
Parting from the Four Attachments: 'if grasping arises, it is not the view'.

historical_debates.name: Gorampa's and Taktsang's critiques and the Gelug replies
historical_debates.accounts: Written polemics rather than a single face-to-face debate: Gorampa's Distinguishing the Views, Taktsang's 'eighteen great burdens', Jamyang Shepa's Great Exposition of Tenets in reply.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds its own view vindicated.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both traditions insist the difference is real and doctrinal.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Gelug speaks of the object ascertained by a reasoning consciousness (a non-affirming negation), Gorampa of the meditative equipoise in which no extreme is grasped — possibly two standpoints on one realisation.
P4-stage: Gorampa himself treats the negation of true existence as a step; the Gelug also holds that in direct realisation emptiness appears without dualistic elaboration.
P5-neyartha: each side reads the other's key citations as provisional.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gelug holds that 'freedom from all extremes' without qualification repeats the error of Hwashang and destroys conventional truth; Gorampa holds that the Gelug qualifier retains a subtle reified emptiness. Neither accepts a merely verbal difference.

question: Are Tsongkhapa's eight 'difficult points' genuinely Candrakīrti's Prāsaṅgika?

sides.position: Prāsaṅgika uniquely rejects an ālaya distinct from the six consciousnesses and reflexive awareness even conventionally, rejects autonomous inference, accepts external objects conventionally, holds that śrāvakas realise the selflessness of phenomena, that grasping at the self of phenomena is an affliction, that disintegration is a functioning thing, and so presents the three times uniquely.
arguments: Each point follows from accepting no inherent existence even conventionally (e.g. karma needs no ālaya because 'disintegratedness' can function).
Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra and Prasannapadā are cited for each.

sides.position: Sakya critics (Taktsang Lotsawa, Gorampa, Shākya Chokden) held several of these to be Tsongkhapa's innovations, charging contradictions (Taktsang's 'eighteen great burdens'): e.g. accepting conventional valid cognition and external objects under the name of Prāsaṅgika, or making disintegration a thing.
arguments: Candrakīrti accepts conventions only as the world accepts them, without analysis.
Positing a disintegratedness that functions reintroduces a quasi-substance.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the dispute concerns which positions are Candrakīrti's.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Gelug systematises what conventional designation requires once inherent existence is denied; the critics speak from the standpoint of the unexamined worldly convention.
P5-neyartha: the disagreement is over which passages of Candrakīrti are definitive.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gelug holds the eight points are Candrakīrti's explicit or implied view; the Sakya critics hold them to be additions.

question: Is the ultimate truth an object of knowledge, and is emptiness realised by valid cognition (perception and inference)?

sides.position: The ultimate truth (emptiness) is an object of knowledge: it is found by a reasoning consciousness analysing the final mode of being, first realised by inference and then directly by yogic perception, in which it appears without dualistic appearance.
arguments: If emptiness could not be known, the path to liberation could not be practised.
Inference ascertains the absence of inherent existence as a non-affirming negation.

sides.position: Emptiness is not realised by perception and inference as Buddhist logicians define them — to say so is the talk of the near-sighted; otherwise all tenet-holders measuring by valid cognition would agree. It is 'seen' by not seeing, non-conceptually; the valid cognitions were set up to refute opponents.
arguments: Disagreement among all logicians shows valid cognition does not settle dharmatā.
Scripture says it is not known by conceptual or non-conceptual knowledge (citing Bhavya).

sides.position: The ultimate is beyond the scope of mind and words; it is not an object of knowledge in the ordinary sense, and is 'known' only as the non-dual state of meditative equipoise (Gorampa).
arguments: An object requires a subject; in the ultimate subject and object are not divided.

reconciliation.explanation: All three agree the direct realisation is non-dual and non-conceptual; they differ on whether that realisation may be called 'knowing an object' and on the role of inference beforehand (standpoint of conventional description vs. of the equipoise itself).
reconciliation.detail: Atiśa's denial targets emptiness as the object of the logicians' two pramāṇas taken dualistically; the Gelug accepts that in direct realisation there is no dualistic appearance ('like water poured into water'), while still classifying emptiness as an object of knowledge conventionally.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gelug insists that denying emptiness is an object of knowledge makes the path unknowable; Gorampa insists that calling it an object reifies it. The reconciliation claims only a shared account of the non-dual realisation, not agreement on the classification.

question: Does a Prāsaṅgika assert any thesis of his own?

sides.position: Prāsaṅgikas have no thesis asserting inherent existence, but they do assert theses conventionally — e.g. that phenomena lack inherent existence — and uphold them with valid cognition; Nāgārjuna's 'I have no thesis' means no thesis that is inherently existent.
arguments: Without any assertion there could be no path, no teaching and no refutation.

sides.position: In ultimate analysis the Mādhyamika holds no thesis at all, following Vigrahavyāvartanī 29; conventional statements are made only in accordance with others' perspective, without ultimate commitment (Gorampa and the earlier Tibetan Prāsaṅgikas).
arguments: Any thesis is an elaboration; the view is freedom from all elaboration.

reconciliation.explanation: Both deny any thesis at the ultimate level and allow statements at the conventional level; they differ on whether conventional assertions are the Mādhyamika's own and established by valid cognition.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gelug holds Gorampa's 'others' perspective' reduces the Madhyamaka to having nothing to teach; the Sakya holds the Gelug's own conventional theses retain grasping.

question: Is conceptual analysis part of meditation, or must all thought be stopped?

sides.position: Analytical meditation is indispensable: faith, renunciation, bodhicitta and the view are produced by analysis; insight arises only when analysis itself induces pliancy; stopping all thought is not realisation of emptiness but a blank state.
arguments: A fainted person would otherwise be realised (Kamalaśīla).
Placement alone does not transform the mind on topics needing conviction.

sides.position: Conceptualisation is great ignorance and saṃsāra itself; after ascertaining by scripture and reasoning that phenomena are unborn, one meditates without conceptualisation (Atiśa).
arguments: Nirvāṇa is the abandoning of all conceptualisation.
The Dhāraṇī of Entering the Non-conceptual.

sides.position: Sakya Paṇḍita: a Mahāmudrā of mere thoughtlessness without the wisdom of empowerment is the cause of animal or formless rebirth; genuine non-conceptual wisdom comes through empowerment and the two stages.
arguments: The 'white self-sufficient remedy' is not the Buddha's teaching.

reconciliation.explanation: All three place reasoned ascertainment before non-conceptual meditation; Atiśa's non-conceptual meditation follows analysis (v60), which is the Gelug sequence of analysis leading to non-dual realisation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gelug denies that non-conceptuality can be produced by merely stopping thought; teachers of direct-introduction methods (outside this unit) would object that analysis is not required for every practitioner.

question: May celibate monastics receive (and practise) the secret and wisdom empowerments?

sides.position: No: the Ādibuddha tantra strongly prohibits the secret and wisdom empowerments for those who keep celibacy; taking them breaks the vow, incurs defeat, leads to the lower realms and yields no accomplishment; with the master's empowerment the celibate may still hear and teach all tantras and perform fire offerings.
arguments: The Ādibuddha tantra's prohibition.
The prātimokṣa vow of celibacy would be broken.

sides.position: Monastics may receive the four empowerments of Highest Yoga Tantra, the higher ones with a visualised wisdom-consort, and practise the completion stage without breaking celibacy; practice with an actual consort belongs only to a very advanced stage and the tradition's monks refrain from it.
arguments: Tsongkhapa kept full monastic discipline while practising Highest Yoga Tantra.
The prohibition concerns literal practice, not receiving the empowerment in visualisation.

reconciliation.explanation: Both forbid the celibate the literal practice; they differ on whether the empowerment itself may be taken in visualised form.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Atiśa's verse states the prohibition of taking the empowerments, not only of practising them; a strict Kadam reading rejects the visualised-consort solution.

notes: The Gelug side is recalled from the tradition's practice; Tsongkhapa's exact wording is not given.

question: Must one hold a prātimokṣa vow to take the bodhisattva vow?

sides.position: Only those who always keep one of the seven kinds of prātimokṣa vow have the fortune for the bodhisattva vow, not others.
arguments: The bodhisattva vow is built on the ethics of restraint.

sides.position: There are two bodhisattva-vow traditions: the one from Asaṅga (Cittamātra) requires a prior prātimokṣa vow; the one from Nāgārjuna and Śāntideva (Madhyamaka) can be given to anyone with the aspiration; each is to be conferred by its own rite (Sakya Paṇḍita).
arguments: Different rites for different recipients; do not mix the procedures.

reconciliation.explanation: Atiśa's condition applies to the rite of the Bodhisattvabhūmi (Asaṅga's tradition), which is the rite he names; the Madhyamaka rite has different entry conditions.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: A strict reading of Atiśa's verse makes the condition general.

notes: The Sakya side is recalled; chapter reference approximate.

question: Is the ultimate one, or divisible (e.g. into a concordant/nominal and an actual ultimate)?

sides.position: The ultimate is only one; dharmatā, established as nothing at all, cannot be two or three (Atiśa).
arguments: What is not established as anything cannot be counted.

sides.position: The ultimate is taught as twofold: the actual ultimate beyond elaboration, and the concordant (nominal) ultimate — the reasoned negation of arising — which accords with it (Bhāviveka, Jñānagarbha).
arguments: The reasoning consciousness's object is called ultimate because it accords with the ultimate.

reconciliation.explanation: The 'concordant ultimate' is a conventional designation for what accords with the ultimate; Atiśa's 'one' concerns dharmatā itself, which the Svātantrikas also hold to be undivided.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded in the texts of this unit; U40 records the Svātantrika side fully.

question: Are universals real entities (the Tibetan debate on Dharmakīrti)?

sides.position: Chapa Chökyi Senge and the Sangphu logicians (Kadam scholastic line) treated certain universals and relations as real (reported by their critics).
arguments: Conceptual cognition would be baseless without real generalities.

sides.position: Sakya Paṇḍita: only particulars are real; universals are conceptual constructs formed by exclusion, as Dharmakīrti taught.
arguments: Only what performs a function is ultimately real.

sides.position: Universals (generally characterised phenomena) exist conventionally as permanent, non-functioning phenomena, though they are not real in the sense of functioning things (Gelug pramāṇa textbooks).
arguments: Existence and reality (functioning) are distinguished.

candidate_readings: P1-level: 'real' as ultimately (functionally) real vs. conventionally existent may dissolve part of the disagreement between the Sakya and Gelug sides.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sakya Paṇḍita's critique targets the reification itself; the Sangphu side is known mainly through critics.

notes: Chapa's position is reported by his critics; see U41 dsp:apoha.

question: Prāsaṅgika against Svātantrika

sides.position: The difference is in the view, not only in method: Svātantrikas accept that phenomena exist by their own character conventionally and therefore use autonomous inferences; Prāsaṅgikas deny this even conventionally and so use consequences and 'other-acknowledged' inferences. Hence Prāsaṅgika's object of negation is subtler.
arguments: The commonly appearing subject required for autonomous inference implies inherent existence.

sides.position: The two differ only in how the view is generated in another's mind — by autonomous inference or by consequence — not in the view realised, which is freedom from elaboration for both (Gorampa).
arguments: The ultimate realised by both is the same freedom from extremes.

notes: Sides contributed by U47; U50 owns the dispute and its reconciliation.

question: Empty of self, or empty of other?

sides.position: Only 'self-emptiness' is correct: every phenomenon, the ultimate included, is empty of its own inherent existence; an ultimate empty only of other (adventitious) things but not of itself would be truly existent and a form of eternalism.
arguments: Emptiness is itself empty.
A truly existent ultimate cannot withstand analysis.

sides.position: Gorampa classes Dolpopa's other-emptiness as 'Madhyamaka of the eternalist extreme'; Shākya Chokden, in contrast, held that self-emptiness is the view for cutting conceptual elaboration and other-emptiness the view for meditative experience, both valid.
arguments: (Gorampa) the ultimate is free of all extremes, including permanence.
(Shākya Chokden) the Maitreya texts' other-emptiness describes the luminous wisdom experienced in meditation.

notes: Sides contributed by U47 (Gelug; Sakya incl. Shākya Chokden); U50 owns, U48 gives the Jonang side.

question: Is there a Mahāmudrā outside tantric empowerment (sūtra or 'white panacea' Mahāmudrā)?

sides.position: Sakya Paṇḍita: the Mahāmudrā taught by the Buddha is only the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages; the present-day 'white self-sufficient remedy' taught without empowerment is the Chinese (Hwashang) Great Perfection under another name, and a fool's meditation on it leads to animal or formless rebirth or the śrāvaka cessation.
arguments: No such Mahāmudrā is found in the tantras.
It repeats the simultaneist teaching rejected at Samye.

sides.position: The Kagyu teach a Mahāmudrā of pointing out the nature of mind that can be introduced on the basis of sūtra (the Ratnagotravibhāga and Maitrīpa's teaching of non-attention), as Gampopa did; later Kagyu scholars answered Sakya Paṇḍita that his target was not their teaching.
arguments: Maitrīpa's amanasikāra teaching is Indian and not Chinese.
The Ratnagotravibhāga's buddha-nature supports a sūtra approach.

sides.position: The First Panchen Lama: Mahāmudrā has a sūtra approach (emptiness of mind as Nāgārjuna taught) and a mantra approach (clear light of great bliss); the various Mahāmudrā instructions converge in one intent.
arguments: The sūtra approach is meditation on emptiness taught by Nāgārjuna.

notes: Sides contributed by U47 (Sakya Paṇḍita; Gelug Mahāmudrā); the Kagyu side is recorded only briefly and is owned by U46.
